catalog_quote: Mbuko is a metrical language. Rhythmic stress is right-headed, and runs right to left. In other words, within a pause phrase the final syllable is stressed, and then every second or third syllable, counting from right to left, is stressed. Feet are made up of two or three syllables, though three is preferred. Heavy (i.e. closed) syllables may count for two rhythmic pulses. It is the final syllable in a foot that is stressed. Metrical stress is difficult to determine phonetically. It seems to be a rhythmic feature, with amplitude helping to distinguish the stressed syllable. Native speakers react to stress primarily on the basis of rhythm, though when asked to pick “stronger” syllables, they may also pick those containing an underlying /a/ vowel. Stress is not a feature of a word, and may occur on any syllable in different contexts. In the following examples bold type denotes a stressed …

new_statements.rule_in_words: Mbuko (a three-level tone language) has no lexical/word stress. Stress is rhythmic and assigned over the pause phrase: the phrase-final syllable is stressed and right-headed feet of two or (preferably) three syllables are built right-to-left from it, with closed syllables optionally counting as two pulses; the same word can be stressed on different syllables in different contexts. Speakers manipulate long/short allomorphs of grammatical markers, epenthetic /a/, schwa retention and verb reduplication to optimise the trisyllabic meter (§7.2-7.6).
new_statements.secondary_stress: No primary/secondary distinction; all foot-final syllables in the pause phrase are described simply as 'stressed' (iterative rhythmic beats every 2nd-3rd syllable leftward from the phrase-final syllable).
new_statements.exceptions: Native speakers asked to pick 'stronger' syllables may also pick syllables containing underlying /a/ (full vowel) rather than schwa; author notes the rules governing metrical choices in normal (non-rhythmic) speech are hard to state (§7.6). §4.6 (p.72) adds that stress units, like the basic phonological word, are two or three syllables long.
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is explicitly the pause phrase, not the word ('Stress is not a feature of a word'). In isolation/citation a word is its own pause phrase, so its final syllable would carry the phrase-final beat, but the author does not frame this as word stress. Language is tonal (3 surface level tones, ch. 5 p.74); stress is treated as independent of tone.
new_statements.identity_note: Source describes Mbuko (mqb, mbuk1243) as spoken around Meri/Doulek, Diamaré, Far North Cameroon; no dialect restriction stated. Not to be confused with the sister description Smith 1999 'Muyang Phonology' (muya1243) in the same SIL Cameroon series / same 2010 print volume.
